summary:
Fire behaves differently in microgravity, creating unique risks for astronauts and spacecraft. Although NASA has collected decades of combustion research, the volume and complexity of this data can make it difficult to find, compare, and apply.

We developed Flame in Freefall, an interactive platform that organizes 24 NASA investigations and more than 1,800 experimental records. Users can search the evidence, compare fuels, oxygen levels, airflow conditions, and sensors, and inspect every result with traceable sources. Source-bounded SI assistance helps translate practical fire-safety questions into relevant research while keeping missing information and uncertainty visible.

The platform also includes an explainable 3D cabin-screening tool. It evaluates user-confirmed materials, ignition sources, vents, oxygen sources, detectors, and suppression equipment to identify relative hotspots and examine detector coverage.

By connecting published evidence with interactive visualization and transparent computational screening, Flame in Freefall makes NASA research more accessible as a starting point for spacecraft design, safety review, and future investigation.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a web-based research and spacecraft fire-safety screening platform. It connects three areas of the challenge: fire prevention, detection, and suppression.

The Evidence Explorer organizes 24 NASA Physical Sciences investigations and more than 1,800 indexed experimental records, including research from BASS, BASS-II, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, and related programs. Users can search by research question or keyword, filter studies by fuel, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, sensor, experiment family, and available evidence, and compare selected investigations side by side. Results include direct source links, supporting records, reported conditions, and warnings when values are missing, ambiguous, or potentially inconsistent.

The optional SI-guided search converts a user’s question into a source-bounded research query. It helps users find relevant evidence without allowing the language model to invent experimental measurements. The system distinguishes published data, user-entered conditions, illustrative coefficients, and unknown values.

Our second major component is an explainable 3D cabin-screening tool. Users can load a GLB spacecraft model, confirm its scale and meshes, and identify materials, ignition sources, vents, oxygen sources, detectors, and suppression equipment. Python and PyTorch evaluate many candidate locations and produce a relative screening index. Each hotspot explains its strongest contributing factors, nearby objects, and detector coverage. Users can move a detector and repeat the analysis using the same candidate locations, making the before-and-after effect reproducible. The result is a research and design-screening aid, not a CFD fire simulation, safety certification, or prediction of a real fire.

A key creative feature is the connection between the two tools. A hotspot can generate an evidence-search handoff containing its location, nearby objects, cabin conditions, and a research question about material flammability, detection, or suppression. This turns a visual screening result into a traceable starting point for deeper research.

We developed the project using React, JavaScript, Vite, and Three.js for the responsive web interface and 3D visualization. Python, FastAPI, and PyTorch support the analysis service, while optional Gemini integration provides source-grounded SI guidance. GitHub supports team development and deployment, and Render hosts the public application. The precomputed cabin demonstration remains available if the live analysis service is temporarily unavailable.

Our team prioritized traceability, repeatability, responsive design, clear instructions, human confirmation of imported geometry, and honest treatment of uncertainty. The intended impact is to help researchers, engineers, students, and mission planners navigate NASA’s combustion evidence more efficiently and identify questions that deserve further testing as human missions extend toward the Moon and Mars.
